qs.q: A 30-year-old man has weight loss, chronic diarrhea, then develops Pneumocystis pneumonia, CMV retinitis, and oral candidiasis. Most likely lab finding?
qs.e: Multiple opportunistic infections (Pneumocystis, CMV, Candida) = AIDS. CD4 count below 200/microliter is the threshold at which AIDS-defining opportunistic infections occur in HIV infection.

ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Pneumocystis pneumonia is a life‑threatening opportunistic infection of the lungs, most common in patients with CD4 counts below 200 cells/µL. It presents with progressive dyspnea, dry cough and fever, and shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates on imaging.

sections.p: Pneumocystis jirovecii is a fungal organism that colonises the alveoli of immunocompromised hosts. In healthy people it is usually harmless, but in those with impaired cell‑mediated immunity it can cause severe pneumonia.
b: It is a fungus, not a bacterium.
It is transmitted by airborne droplets.

sections.p: The organism has a cystic form that is resistant to environmental stresses and a trophic form that invades alveolar epithelium. It lacks a cell wall, which explains its resistance to many antifungals.
b: Cystic form is the infectious stage.

sections.p: Inhalation of airborne cysts leads to colonisation of the alveoli. In immunocompetent hosts, the immune system clears the organism; in immunocompromised hosts, the trophic form proliferates, causing alveolar damage.
b: No person‑to‑person contact beyond airborne spread.

sections.p: Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) is characterised by progressive dyspnea, dry cough, low‑grade fever and hypoxia. Chest imaging shows diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates.
b: Occurs mainly in HIV/AIDS (CD4 <200), but also in transplant recipients, malignancy, and other immunosuppressive states.

sections.p: Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion, imaging and microbiological confirmation. The gold standard is detection of the organism in respiratory specimens by microscopy or PCR.
b: If BAL unavailable, sputum microscopy or PCR can be used, but sensitivity is lower.

t.b: Shows ground‑glass opacities; indicates interstitial involvement.
Detects cysts/trophs; positive result confirms PCP.
Highly sensitive; positive in most cases, especially when microscopy is negative.
Elevated LDH suggests alveolar damage; supports diagnosis when imaging and microbiology are equivocal.

sections.p: First‑line therapy is high‑dose cotrimoxazole, chosen for its dual antibacterial and antifungal activity and proven efficacy. Adjunctive corticosteroids are added when hypoxia is severe.
b: Cotrimoxazole is preferred because it covers the organism and reduces mortality.

sections.p: Remember that PCP is a fungal infection, not bacterial. In HIV patients with CD4 <200, a high index of suspicion is required. The key diagnostic test is BAL microscopy or PCR.
b: Cotrimoxazole is the drug of choice; steroids improve outcomes in severe disease.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe shortness of breath, hypoxia (SpO2 <90%), or sudden worsening of symptoms

faq.a: No, it is a fungus with a cystic and trophic form.

faq.q: Can it be transmitted from person to person?
faq.a: Yes, via airborne droplets, but it usually only causes disease in immunocompromised hosts.

faq.q: What is the most common risk factor?
faq.a: HIV infection with CD4 count below 200 cells/µL.
